Welcome

If you would like to view this content please Allow Cookies Cookie Settings
St. Edmund's is a welcoming and nurturing environment, where each individual is supported to develop morally, spiritually, socially, culturally and academically. Our extended community, through our Christian values of Love, Courage, Trust and Respect encourage each other in faith to ‘Let your light shine.’ (Matthew 5).
We are delighted to welcome you to St. Edmund's Church of England Primary School, a village school nestled in the heart of West Kingsdown village, where children explore, learn, create and grow together. We are delighted to be part of the Compass Federation, a group of three schools, which includes St. Paul's in Swanley Village and Dunton Green Primary School. We work closely together under an Executive Headteacher and Governing Body.
We believe that every child should succeed in our school and thrive due to excellent teaching and high expectations. Every child’s contribution to the school is valued, and we recognise and celebrate every child’s achievements and milestones. Our school has a caring family ethos and, with parents and staff working together, we support each other in helping everyone's light to shine.
Our Christian values are the foundation of our school, and they run through every aspect of life here at St. Edmund's. We work closely with our parish church, which is tucked away in West Kingsdown woods, and the pupils walk to the church to attend Harvest Festivals, Remembrance services, Christingle services, Bible presentations for our Year 2 pupils and Year 6 Leavers' Services.
Thank you for visiting our website. We hope you find it informative and that it reflects the wonderful education and diverse opportunities our children experience at St. Edmund's.

Religious Education
What is covered during RE lessons?
The school follows the Kent Agreed Syllabus supported by Rochester Diocesan materials. The agreed syllabus follows the legal requirement for religious education to reflect the fact that the religious traditions in Great Britain are in the main Christian, while taking account of the teachings and practices of the other principal religions represented in Great Britain.
At St. Edmund's, pupils study Christian RE topics in every year group. Pupils are taught about the main traditions, practices and beliefs of the religions, but will also have the opportunity to relate the key concepts covered to their own experiences and explore their own beliefs and questions of meaning. Each year group has a different RE unit of work every half term.
When is RE taught?
RE is taught weekly in each class and year group for an hour a week. There are also other opportunities during the year where other religious education is taught through a more thematic approach such as Christmas and Easter.
What should I do if I want to withdraw my child from RE or collective worship?
Parents have the right to choose whether or not to withdraw their child from RE without influence from the school, although a school should ensure parents or carers are informed of this right and are aware of the educational objectives and content of the RE syllabus. In this way, parents can make an informed decision. Where parents have requested that their child is withdrawn, their right must be respected, and where RE is integrated in the curriculum, the Headteacher will need to discuss the arrangements with the parents or carers to explore how the child’s withdrawal can be best accommodated. If pupils are withdrawn from RE, schools have a duty to supervise them, though not to provide additional teaching or to incur extra cost. Pupils will usually remain on school premises.

pageCache.pageTitle: St. Edmund's Church of England Primary School - Academic Results

Academic Results
Our Outcomes
At St. Edmund’s, we are proud of the progress and achievements of our children. Our assessment outcomes reflect many areas of real strength, alongside our continued commitment to improving outcomes for every pupil.
An excellent start in Early Years
Our youngest children achieve exceptionally well.
In 2025–26, 90% of children achieved a Good Level of Development at the end of Reception, compared with approximately 72% nationally. This represents a significant strength for the school and demonstrates the strong foundations children develop during their first year with us.
Exceptional multiplication knowledge
Our Year 4 pupils achieved outstanding outcomes in the national Multiplication Tables Check.
83% of pupils achieved full marks – 25 out of 25 – compared with approximately 44% nationally. The average score was 24.8 out of 25, substantially above the national average of approximately 21.6.
This strong knowledge of number facts provides children with an important foundation for increasingly complex mathematics as they move through the school.
Strong reading and writing outcomes
At the end of Key Stage 2, 78% of pupils achieved the expected standard in Reading, above the national figure of 75%.
In Writing, 74% achieved the expected standard, also slightly above the national figure of 73%.
We are particularly pleased to see the continued improvement in Reading, with the proportion reaching the expected standard increasing from 65% in 2023 to 78% in 2026.
Strong achievement in Science
Science is another area of strength. In 2025–26, 93% of Year 6 pupils achieved the expected standard, compared with 82% nationally.
Building confident readers
While the proportion of Year 1 pupils reaching the expected standard in the Phonics Screening Check remains an area we are continuing to strengthen, pupils demonstrate strong catch-up as they progress through the school.
By the end of Year 2, 92% of pupils had met the phonics standard, slightly above the national figure of approximately 91%.
This reflects our commitment to identifying children who need additional support and helping them to become confident, successful readers.
Continuing to improve
We are ambitious for every child at St. Edmund’s.
Our results show significant strengths, particularly in Early Years, reading, writing, science and multiplication fluency. We also recognise where outcomes need to improve further, particularly in aspects of mathematics, grammar, punctuation and spelling, and the proportion of pupils reaching the higher standards at Key Stage 2.
These areas form part of our ongoing school improvement work. Through high-quality teaching, careful assessment and timely support, we are committed to ensuring that every child is given the opportunity to flourish and achieve their very best.

Remote Learning
We hope that your child can be with us in school every day to access learning. However, in exceptional circumstances, this may not always be possible. The following information should help you to ensure that your child can access learning until they can return to lessons at school.
If your child is unable to be in school with us, but is well enough to learn, please follow the following steps:
Send a message to your child's class teacher via Dojo. They will be able to provide you with a suggested timetable for your child’s learning. Please do not hesitate to email or ring the school if you have any questions.
Check our Curriculum overviews on the website.
There are also many helpful websites which your child can access to support them with their learning at home:
Oak Academy has a wide range of lessons available for all curriculum subjects.
BBC Bitesize You will find great videos to support learning across a range of subjects
TTRS Times Tables Rockstars is fantastic for regular practice of times tables.
How can parents support their children with remote learning?
To best support your child’s online learning and progress, we recommend the following:
Make sure your child has the best distraction-free environment possible to learn in.
Check your child’s engagement with their learning. Asking your child the following questions will help you connect with what they are learning:
What have you been learning about today?
Can you show me the learning you are most proud of?
What learning will you be doing next?
Keep in contact with the school, asking questions if things are difficult. We are here to help you.

Our Curriculum
Our Curriculum is about: • connecting: seeing relationships and combining in new ways • risking: having the self-confidence and freedom to fail and keep trying • envisaging: being original and imaginative about what might be • analysing: asking critical and challenging questions • thinking: taking time for reflection • interacting: sharing ideas and collaborating • varying: testing options and trying in different ways • elaborating: exploring and fiddling and doing the unnecessary to perfect In Key Stage 1, we use the Read, Write, Inc scheme for Phonics and to teach reading. Key Stage 1 are taught through play and continuous provision. Children are set learning challenges throughout the week, linked to a topic that allows the children to work independently on tasks that they are interested in and skilled adults move their learning on.
Religion and belief have become more visible in public life in recent years, making it important that all pupils should have an opportunity to engage in RE. However, the parent of a pupil at a community, foundation or voluntary school (or pupils themselves if they are aged 18 or over) may request that they be excused from all or part of the religious education (RE) provided. Parents who wish to withdraw their children from RE should be aware of its aims and what is covered in the RE curriculum and that they are given the opportunity to discuss this if they wish. It should be made clear whether the withdrawal is from the whole RE curriculum or specific parts of it. No reasons need be given

pageCache.text:
Collective Worship
What is collective worship?
Collective worship is a special time during the school day, where pupils are given the space and opportunity to reflect, respond and revere. There is an act of Collective Worship every day for the whole school community. Our aim is that our worship is inclusive, invitational and inspiring. We will often include the use of music, a candle, a time of silence and a prayer to offer a focus for pupils.
At our school, this will include the use of songs, music, stories and readings familiar to those of a Christian faith, and promoting the values that Christians believe to be important. We explore the importance of wise words in helping us all to let our light shine.

pageCache.pageTitle: St. Edmund's Church of England Primary School - Forest School
pageCache.text:
Forest School
Forest School is a child-led approach to learning that incorporates children’s right to play, to access the outdoor environment and to feel success.
Forest School is a unique way of building independence and self-esteem in young children, exposing them to the natural world at a time when it is vital for children to understand their impact on the environment. It is a child-centred and child-led programme that provides the opportunity for the children to use their personal learning style to complete various activities.
Forest School is an opportunity for the children at St. Edmund's to have new, creative experiences in the outdoor environment safely. Children will have opportunities to learn about the natural environment, how to handle risks and most importantly to use their own initiative to solve problems and co-operate with others.
Through purposeful and careful planning of Forest School experiences, we strive to increase self-esteem, improve children’s concentration, attendance, behaviour and academic achievement.
We aim to foster a love and respect for the natural world through stimulating natural learning experiences, inspiring children to value biodiversity and develop a strong understanding of how to promote environmental sustainability. The children will experience a minimum of six consecutive sessions in the Forest School in order to immerse themselves in nature and deepen their knowledge and understanding of the flora, fauna and living things that surrounds them in their local environment. The Forest School space will be utilised all year round, with lessons adapted to compliment the ever-changing conditions, resources and challenges of the natural world through the seasons.
At St. Edmund's, we put the children's needs at the heart of all our provision and Forest School only continues to enhance this ethos. Our Forest School promotes cultural diversity, ensuring everyone feels valued and that individuality is celebrated. We are highly confident that Forest School provision will not only compliment and extend the curriculum, but also nurture children to become successful lifelong learners and happy, fulfilled adults who can make positive choices about their futures.
Forest School learning experiences create endless opportunities for cross-curricular links to Science, Mathematics, English, Geography and Art.
Forest School experiences encourage children to develop their self-knowledge, self-esteem and self-confidence through respectful interactions with others and the natural environment. Working as a team to solve problems, children will develop and foster communication and negotiation skills. These skills prepare the children for the world both inside and outside of school.

pageCache.pageTitle: St. Edmund's Church of England Primary School - Justice and Responsibility
pageCache.text:
Justice and Responsibility
Justice, Responsibility and Courageous Advocacy
At St. Edmund’s, our Christian vision calls us to “Let your light shine” (Matthew 5:16). We believe that each person has been given gifts, talents and a voice that can be used not only for themselves, but to bring light, hope and positive change to the lives of others.
Our values of Love, Courage, Trust and Respect help our children understand that being part of a Christian community brings responsibilities. We want pupils to notice the world around them, recognise when something is unfair or unjust, and have the confidence and compassion to respond.
Through our spirituality curriculum, children are encouraged to look through Windows, reflect through Mirrors and step through Doors. Justice, responsibility, service and courageous advocacy provide important opportunities for pupils to step through those Doors and put their beliefs and values into action.
What is courageous advocacy?
A courageous advocate is someone who is prepared to stand up for what is right, speak up for others and take action to make a difference.
At St. Edmund’s, we want our children to understand that their age does not prevent them from creating change. Whether they are helping someone within our school community, supporting a local cause, raising awareness of a national issue or thinking about challenges facing people across the world, every child can allow their light to shine.
Children learn that courageous advocacy is not simply about raising money. It begins with asking questions:
Why is it happening?
What could we do about it?
How can we use our voices, choices and actions to make a difference?
Through collective worship, Religious Education, PSHE and the wider curriculum, pupils explore issues including poverty, inequality, homelessness, conflict, discrimination, environmental responsibility and the needs of their local community.
They are encouraged to listen to different perspectives, develop empathy and consider how Christian teachings about love, justice, compassion and service might influence the way they respond.
Turning belief into action
Throughout their time at St. Edmund’s, children have opportunities to translate what they have learned into meaningful action.
supporting local, national and international charities;
collecting food and other essential items for people in need;
raising awareness of issues that matter to them;
organising fundraising activities;
supporting our local community and church;
caring for the environment;
writing to people in positions of influence;
leading projects and campaigns within school; and
identifying ways in which our school community itself can become fairer, kinder and more sustainable.
Wherever possible, initiatives are not simply chosen for our children. We encourage pupils to identify issues that matter to them, suggest ways of responding and take an active role in making those ideas happen.
Justice and responsibility
We want pupils to understand that justice means more than treating everybody in exactly the same way. It means recognising the dignity and value of every person and thinking carefully about what people need in order to flourish.
Responsibility means recognising that each of us has a part to play.
Our children learn that seemingly small choices — including how we treat someone, what we say, what we buy, what we waste, what we protect and whether we speak up — can have an impact on other people and on the world around us.
This reflects our Christian understanding that we are called to love our neighbours and to use what we have been given in the service of others.
Caring for God’s world
Responsibility also extends to the natural world.
Through curriculum learning, outdoor education and practical environmental action, pupils consider their responsibility as stewards of God’s creation. They learn about issues such as climate change, biodiversity, waste and sustainability and consider practical ways in which individuals and communities can respond.
Children are encouraged to recognise that caring for creation is not something separate from our Christian vision; it is another way in which we can allow our light to shine.
Making a difference
Our aim is for children to leave St. Edmund’s believing that they are not too young to make a difference.
We want them to become thoughtful and compassionate citizens who notice injustice, think critically about the world around them and have the courage to act.
By showing Love, demonstrating Courage, building Trust and treating others with Respect, our pupils learn that they can help the lights of others to shine too.
In doing so, they discover that “Let your light shine” is not simply something we say. It is something we are called to live.

Our Learning
St. Edmund's has both a predominantly single-form entry classroom structure meaning that all year groups are taught on their own in curriculum year groups.
The curriculum is all the planned activities that we organise in order to promote learning and personal growth and development in preparation for life in Modern Britain. It includes not only the formal requirements of the National Curriculum, but also any other activity organised by school, for example, extra-curricular activities and any other activities designed to enrich the experience of the children. There is also a ‘hidden’ element to the curriculum which includes what the children learn from their school environment, the way they are treated and how they are expected to behave.

Our PTA
Our PTA work closely with the school to ensure that we fundraise to the maximum. Being such a small school we rely on funds being raised at our events and functions.
We have lots of exciting events to look forward to across the year and all volunteers would be very much appreciated, please let any of the committee members know if you’re free to help at any of the events shown below.
The role of the PTA is to top up on the government funding given to the school. We do this by holding various fundraising events throughout the year, the most traditional are the Summer Fayre and Christmas Fayre. We also hold discos for the children, non-uniform days, quizzes, an Easter egg hunt, competitions and sales events.
As you can imagine, a lot of hard work goes into planning these events, and the PTA meet to discuss them as regularly as possible. All parents are encouraged to attend PTA meetings when possible to bring in fresh new ideas and to help with implementing them. Joining the PTA doesn’t mean making a long-term commitment. Often we will ask for help to run events like the discos, movie nights and fayres and this can be done on a one off basis or regularly depending on how much time you can commit. You don’t even have to attend every meeting. There are so many ways you could help.

Our extended community, through our Christian values of Love, Courage, Trust and Respect encourage each other in faith to ‘Let your light shine.’ (Matthew 5).
We value every child, ensuring that they develop their individual talents and skills to become happy and successful learners, founded upon Christian values and practice, within our caring school community.
Within the Christian ethos of our school we aim to –
Value each and every child, enabling them to achieve their best in all aspects of school life.
Encourage children to develop into happy, independent and self-motivated young people.
Provide a stimulating and safe environment.
Build a strong partnership between school and parents/carers through a welcoming approach that promotes mutual respect and the highest standards of discipline.
Continue our strong and well established links with the Church and wider community that provide the foundations for spiritual and moral development as well as a passion for lifelong learning.

Safeguarding Pupils
Keeping children safe at St. Edmund’s
At St. Edmund’s Church of England Primary School, the safety and wellbeing of every child is our highest priority.
We are committed to providing a safe, caring and supportive environment in which children can learn, develop and flourish. Everyone who works at, visits or volunteers at our school has a responsibility to help keep children safe.
Safeguarding is everyone’s responsibility.
We work closely with children, families and other professionals to:
Our safeguarding arrangements are informed by statutory guidance, including Keeping Children Safe in Education and Working Together to Safeguard Children.
Our Safeguarding Team
If you have a concern about the safety or welfare of a child, please speak to a member of our safeguarding team.
Designated Safeguarding Lead (DSL) James Johnson – Headteacher
Deputy Designated Safeguarding Leads (DDSLs) Ben Hulme – Executive Headteacher Rob Sinclair-Harris William Ledger Molly Elvidge
Safeguarding Governor Hilary Wilder
The school’s current safeguarding page identifies Mr Johnson as DSL, with Mr Hulme, Mr Ledger, Mr Harris and Miss Elvidge as Deputy DSLs, and Hilary Wilder as the governor responsible for safeguarding.
You can contact the school safeguarding team through the school office:
Telephone: 01474 853484 Email: office@st-edmunds.kent.sch.uk
If you are worried about a child, please tell us. No concern is too small to share.
What should I do if I am worried about a child?
If you are concerned about something you have seen or heard, or about a change in a child’s appearance, behaviour or wellbeing, please speak to the Designated Safeguarding Lead or one of the Deputy Designated Safeguarding Leads as soon as possible.
You do not need to be certain that a child is being harmed before raising a concern.
If a child tells you something that concerns you:
If you believe a child is in immediate danger, call 999.
listen carefully and take them seriously;
remain calm and reassuring;
do not investigate or ask leading questions;
record the concern accurately; and
Concerns outside school
You do not have to contact the school before reporting a safeguarding concern.
If you are worried that a child may be at risk of harm, you can contact Kent Children’s Social Care directly.
Kent Children’s Social Care: 03000 41 11 11 Monday to Friday, 9am–5pm
Out of hours: 03000 41 91 91
If a child is in immediate danger, always call 999.
Concerns about an adult working with children
We take all concerns about the conduct of adults working or volunteering in school seriously.
If you have a concern about the behaviour of a member of staff, volunteer or another adult working with children at St. Edmund’s, you should report this to the Headteacher as soon as possible.
If the concern relates to the Headteacher, it should be reported to the Executive Headteacher.
If the concern relates to the Executive Headteacher, it should be reported to the Chair of Governors.
Concerns will be managed in accordance with statutory safeguarding guidance and, where appropriate, advice will be sought from the Local Authority Designated Officer (LADO).
Online Safety
Technology is an important part of children’s learning and their lives. We teach children how to use technology safely, responsibly and respectfully and how to seek help when something online makes them worried or uncomfortable.
Online safeguarding includes protecting children from risks relating to:
The school has appropriate filtering and monitoring systems in place to help protect children when using school technology and internet-connected devices. These arrangements are reviewed regularly as part of our wider safeguarding responsibilities.
We also work with parents and carers to help children develop safe and healthy habits when using technology at home and at school.
If you are concerned about something that has happened online, please speak to a member of our safeguarding team.
online content;
contact with other people;
their own or others’ online conduct; and
online commercial risks.
Child-on-child abuse
Children can sometimes cause harm to other children.
We recognise that child-on-child abuse can take many forms, including bullying, physical abuse, sexual harassment, sexual violence, harmful sexual behaviour and abuse that takes place online.
We do not dismiss harmful behaviour as ‘banter’, ‘part of growing up’ or ‘just having a laugh’.
Children are encouraged to speak to a trusted adult whenever something makes them feel unsafe or uncomfortable. All concerns are taken seriously and responded to appropriately.
Preventing radicalisation
Protecting children from the risk of radicalisation and extremism forms part of our wider safeguarding responsibilities.
We help children develop the knowledge and skills they need to think critically, understand different perspectives, challenge prejudice and keep themselves safe.
Staff are trained to recognise and respond to concerns that a child may be vulnerable to radicalisation. Any such concerns are managed through our established safeguarding procedures and, where necessary, in partnership with other agencies.
Attendance and safeguarding
Regular school attendance is important for children’s education, wellbeing and safety.
We recognise that changes in attendance, patterns of absence or children missing education can sometimes be indicators of wider safeguarding concerns.
We therefore monitor attendance carefully and work with children and families to understand and address barriers to regular attendance.
Where necessary, we work with other agencies to ensure children receive the right help and support.
Operation Encompass
St. Edmund’s Church of England Primary School is part of Operation Encompass.
Operation Encompass is a partnership between schools and the police that helps schools provide timely support to children who have experienced or been exposed to domestic abuse.
Where the police attend an incident of domestic abuse involving a child connected with our school, relevant information may be shared securely with trained members of our safeguarding team before the start of the next school day.
This enables us to provide appropriate support and understanding for the child when they arrive at school.
Information received through Operation Encompass is treated sensitively and confidentially and is managed in accordance with our safeguarding procedures.
Safer recruitment and visitors
We follow statutory safer recruitment procedures when appointing staff and engaging volunteers.
Appropriate checks are undertaken according to the role being carried out, including Disclosure and Barring Service checks where required.
All visitors must report to the school office, sign in and follow the school’s safeguarding and visitor procedures while on site.
Visitors must wear the identification provided by the school and must not take photographs or recordings of children unless specifically authorised to do so.
Helping children to keep themselves safe
Safeguarding is embedded throughout school life and our curriculum.
We teach children, in an age-appropriate way, about:
We want every child at St. Edmund’s to know that there are adults who will listen to them, take them seriously and help them.
This sits naturally alongside the school’s wider Christian ethos of helping every child to flourish and “Let your light shine.”
healthy and respectful relationships;
recognising unsafe or worrying situations;
boundaries and consent;
online safety;
bullying and discrimination;
seeking help;
trusted adults;
personal safety; and
how and when to speak up.
Working with families
Strong relationships with parents and carers are an important part of keeping children safe.
We aim to work openly and constructively with families and will usually discuss concerns with parents or carers.
There may, however, be circumstances where we need to seek advice or make a referral to another agency before speaking to a parent or carer, particularly where doing so could place a child at greater risk or compromise a safeguarding investigation.
Our first consideration will always be the safety and welfare of the child.

Spiritual Development
As a church school we are concerned with the development of people’s mind, body and soul. We believe that spirituality should influence all areas of education and life, therefore we aim that all areas of the curriculum contribute to pupils’ spiritual development. Spiritual development relates to fundamental questions about the meaning and purpose of life which affect everyone, and is not dependent on a religious affiliation.
Spiritual development is not about becoming, more spiritual, it is about realising or becoming more and more aware of one’s natural, innate spirituality. This is sometimes a slow and gradual process, at other times there might be significant stages of realisation, which are part of the ongoing ‘developing’ process. People don’t reach a finished state of spiritual development, but participate in the ongoing process of spiritual realisation.
How we provide children with openings for spiritual development:
WINDOWS: giving children opportunities to become aware of the world in new ways; to wonder about life’s ‘WOWs’ (things that are amazing) and ‘OWs’ (things that bring us up short). In this children are learning about ‘life in all its fullness.'
MIRRORS: giving children opportunities to reflect on their experiences; to meditate on life’s big questions and to consider some possible answers. In this they are learning from life by exploring their own insights and perspectives and those of others.
DOORS: giving children opportunities to respond to all of this; to do something creative as a means of expressing, applying and further developing their thoughts and convictions. In this they are learning to live by putting into action what they are coming to believe and value.
Therefore, our curriculum has strands permeating it like in a stick of rock - Christian Values and opportunities for spiritual development. We seek to provide occasions for people of all spiritual styles – word, symbol, emotion and action. This encourages children and adults to develop an understanding of the spiritual character of themselves and others. This is why we offer the range we do, for example Creative Prayer Days, Peace Garden, Active Church and Traditional Church.
